patient.title: Cisplatin + etoposide with radiotherapy
patient.purpose: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy work together to treat limited-stage small-cell lung cancer. Your team explains the aim and why this combined treatment is suitable for you.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with cell copying. Fluids and kidney checks help reduce harm to healthy tissue.
agents.watch: Report poor fluid intake, reduced urine, ringing in the ears or numbness.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide blocks an enzyme cells need while copying DNA. The route and prescribed amount differ between infusion and capsules; they are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.
visual: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, severe mouth soreness or vomiting.

phases.label: Radiotherapy alongside chemotherapy
phases.detail: Usually begins with cycle 1; later start may be appropriate. The radiation team confirms dose, number of visits and timing. A chemotherapy delay does not automatically mean radiation stops.

patient.title: Weekly carboplatin + paclitaxel with radiotherapy
patient.purpose: Chemotherapy is given alongside radiotherapy to treat stage III non-small-cell lung cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim and choices.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises structures needed for cell division. It can also affect nerves, blood cells and healthy tissues. Premedicines help reduce infusion reactions.
agents.watch: Report numbness, tingling, muscle/joint pain or new breathing symptoms.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with cell copying. Its dose uses kidney filtration and target exposure(AUC), not a fixed number of milligrams.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bleeding, vomiting or allergy symptoms.

phases.label: Seven weekly chemotherapy treatments
phases.detail: Both medicines are given by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside a separate radiotherapy course. The plan may change for side effects or test results. Further chemotherapy after radiotherapy is a separate decision.

phases.label: Radiation course
phases.detail: Radiation is given during the chemotherapy course. Its dose, number of fractions and precise timing are prescribed by radiation oncology. A chemotherapy delay does not automatically stop radiation.

phases.label: After chemoradiation
phases.detail: Your team reviews recovery and response. NCCP describes optional separate two-cycle carboplatin/paclitaxel consolidation under00304; it is not automatically included and any next treatment needs a separate prescription.

timeline.label: Paclitaxel then carboplatin
timeline.text: One weekly chemotherapy visit after blood tests and premedicines.

timeline.label: Symptoms and separate RT plan
timeline.text: Continue the written radiation and support plan. Symptoms may occur on any day; this is not a radiation-fraction calendar.

day_groups.action: Tell staff immediately about flushing, breathing trouble, pain or swelling during infusion.

day_groups.body: Use the anti-sickness medicines prescribed for these days. Radiation visits may continue on their own schedule.

day_groups.action: Report problems before the next dose; do not wait if acutely unwell.

support.title: Weekly medicines before treatment
support.text: Paclitaxel needs premedicines to reduce allergic reactions. The first week and later weeks can differ. Your team also provides anti-sickness medicines for carboplatin; do not double up steroid doses.

support.title: Eating, swallowing and breathing
support.text: Chest radiation can make swallowing sore. Ask early for pain relief and nutrition support. New breathlessness, cough or inability to drink needs urgent advice, even after the course finishes.

support.title: Nerves and aches
support.text: Tell the team about numbness, tingling or muscle/joint pain before each weekly visit. Follow the agreed pain-relief plan and check before starting medicines or supplements.

patient.title: Carboplatin + etoposide + chest radiotherapy
patient.purpose: Chemotherapy and chest radiotherapy work together to treat lung cancer. Your team will explain the aim, possible benefit and alternatives for you.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin damages the DNA that cancer cells need to divide. It can also affect healthy cells.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bleeding, reduced urine, hearing changes or tingling.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with an enzyme used to copy and repair DNA. This can stop cancer cells growing and can also lower healthy blood counts.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, a sore mouth or feeling faint during an infusion.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection

agents.name: Chest radiotherapy
agents.explanation: Radiotherapy directs radiation at the planned chest area. Its appointments and dose are set by the radiation oncology team.
agents.watch: Report painful swallowing, poor intake, skin changes, new cough or breathlessness.
risks: Sore skin in the treated area
Cough or breathing changes during or after treatment

agents.name: Docetaxel
agents.explanation: Docetaxel prevents normal rearrangement of the cell structures needed for division. It affects cancer cells and can also suppress blood cells, irritate nerves and cause fluid retention.
visual: Healthy tissues may also be affected
agents.watch: Fever or feeling suddenly unwell needs urgent advice. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms or pain.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Hair loss, fatigue and mouth soreness
Severe bowel inflammation and infusion-site injury

agents.name: Nintedanib
agents.mechanism: Blocks VEGF, FGF and PDGF receptor signalling
agents.explanation: Nintedanib blocks several signals involved in the growth of blood vessels that support a tumour. Its effects can also cause diarrhoea, liver changes, bleeding and wound-healing problems.
visual: Blocks VEGF, FGF and PDGF receptor signalling
Healthy tissues may also be affected
agents.watch: Call early for diarrhoea or poor fluid intake; report bleeding, yellow eyes, dark urine, severe tummy pain or new neurological symptoms urgently.
risks: Bleeding, blood clots and high blood pressure

Rare bowel perforation, ischaemic colitis or PRES
